nextSteps.title: What's Next
nextSteps.subtitle: Your will is ready to be signed. Follow these steps to execute it properly.
nextSteps.validityBody:
Creating your will in this app is an important first step.

In most Canadian provinces, a will becomes legally enforceable once it is printed, signed by you, and witnessed according to your province's requirements.

Some provinces allow limited electronic wills, while others still require physical signatures and witnesses.

Requirements vary by province. Completing the signing steps ensures your wishes are legally recognized after your passing.
nextSteps.checklist4: Have it witnessed as required in your province
nextSteps.checklist5: Store it somewhere safe and accessible
nextSteps.checklistHelper: Once the signed version is uploaded, your vault will unlock for secure storage.
nextSteps.privacyBody: All information you provide is encrypted and stored securely. We never share your personal details.
nextSteps.professionalBody:
Using a law firm to sign your will is optional and not required in most cases.

Some people choose professional signing for added peace of mind or convenience. Others prefer to complete the signing themselves using witnesses they trust.

Both options are valid.
nextSteps.feature3: Confirmation that signing meets provincial requirements
nextSteps.pricing: Pricing varies by province based on local law firm rates and requirements.
nextSteps.pricingNote: This service is optional and not required to make your will valid. Our team will connect you with an appropriate law firm in your province.
nextSteps.rememberBody: You can complete the signing process yourself at no additional cost. Professional assistance is available if you prefer extra guidance.
nextSteps.confirmationBody: Thank you for your interest in professional signing assistance. Our team will review your request and contact you shortly to connect you with an appropriate law firm in your province.

expatProvince.q1: Which province do I choose if I live abroad?
expatProvince.a1: The province where your property in Canada is. Its law decides how that property passes and how the Will is signed.
expatProvince.q2: What if I own property in more than one province?
expatProvince.a2: Choose the province where most of it is. Property in another province may need extra steps, so it's worth asking a lawyer.
expatProvince.q3: What if I move back to Canada?
expatProvince.a3: Make a new Will that covers everything you own. An expat Will only deals with your property here.

expatPreviousWills.q1: Why can't I cancel all my previous Wills?
expatPreviousWills.a1: Because your Will where you live still has to cover everything outside Canada. Cancelling it would leave that property with no Will.
expatPreviousWills.q2: Does this Will change my Will from home?
expatPreviousWills.a2: No. It deals only with your property here. Tell whoever keeps your other Will that this one exists, so the two don't overlap.
expatPreviousWills.q3: What if I don't have a Will where I live?
expatPreviousWills.a3: This Will still covers your property here. For everything else, make a Will where you live, with a local lawyer.

expatForeignWills.q1: Why is my home country already listed?
expatForeignWills.a1: An expat Will always keeps your Will from where you live. Listing it tells your executor it exists and which property it covers.
expatForeignWills.q2: Should a lawyer check my Will from home?
expatForeignWills.a2: Yes. A lawyer there can make sure its wording doesn't cancel this Will by accident. Many Wills cancel all earlier Wills unless they say otherwise.
expatForeignWills.a3: Yes. Add any other country where you have a Will, so it's kept too.

expatExecutors.q1: Can my executor live outside Canada?
expatExecutors.a1: Yes, but it's harder. A court may ask them to post a bond, and they may need a lawyer or agent here to deal with banks and land records.
expatExecutors.q2: What extra tax steps are there?
expatExecutors.a2: When executors live abroad the estate can be treated as non-resident for tax. That can mean withholding tax and clearance certificates from the Canada Revenue Agency before property is sold or passed on.
expatExecutors.q3: What if everyone I trust lives abroad?
expatExecutors.a3: You can name one of them with someone in Canada, or a trust company here. Talk to a lawyer about the best mix.

expatGuardians.q1: Why are guardians off in an expat Will?
expatGuardians.a1: Children are usually cared for where they live, so guardians are normally named in your Will from home. This Will deals with your property here.
expatGuardians.q2: When should I name guardians here too?
expatGuardians.a2: If your children might live in Canada, or you have no Will where you live. Name the same people in both Wills so they don't disagree.
expatGuardians.q3: What if my two Wills name different guardians?
expatGuardians.a3: A court would have to decide. Keep the choices the same, and update both Wills together.

expatEstate.q1: What counts as property in Canada?
expatEstate.a1: A home or land here, Canadian bank and investment accounts, and belongings kept here. Your Will where you live covers the rest.
expatEstate.q2: Can I give away property abroad in this Will?
expatEstate.a2: No. Leave it to your Will where you live. Giving the same thing away in both Wills would cause a conflict.
expatEstate.q3: Are there taxes when a non-resident's property passes on?
expatEstate.a3: Canada can tax gains on property here, such as a home or land, when you die. A lawyer or accountant can help you plan for it.

financialPoa.q1: What does a financial power of attorney do?
financialPoa.a1: It names someone you trust, your attorney, to manage your money and property if you can't: paying bills, banking, looking after your home. It ends when you die, and your Will takes over.
financialPoa.q2: Does my attorney have to be a lawyer?
financialPoa.a2: No. "Attorney" just means the person you appoint. Most people choose a spouse, an adult child or a close friend.
financialPoa.a3: Depending on your province and your choice, either as soon as it's signed or only once you can no longer manage your affairs. In Québec, a protection mandate only takes effect once a court confirms it.
financialPoa.q4: What if I don't have one?
financialPoa.a4: Your family may have to go to court, or a public guardian may manage your affairs. That can be slow and costly.
financialPoa.q5: Can I choose the same people as in my Will?
financialPoa.a5: Yes. VeeWill uses the people you've already added, so you only enter them once.

healthDirective.q1: What is a health care directive?
healthDirective.a1: It names who makes health and personal care decisions for you if you can't, and records the care you would or wouldn't want. It's often called a living will.
healthDirective.q2: Why does my province call it something else?
healthDirective.a2: Each province has its own law and name: a Power of Attorney for Personal Care in Ontario, a Representation Agreement in British Columbia, a Personal Directive in Alberta. VeeWill uses your province's name.
healthDirective.a3: Yes. You can say whether you'd want treatment that only prolongs life when there's no reasonable hope of recovery, or leave it to your decision-maker.
healthDirective.a4: Someone who knows your values, will speak up for you and can be reached quickly. Ask them first.
healthDirective.a5: Your decision-maker and your doctor. Tell your family where the original is kept.

poaAboutYou.q1: Why do you use the details from my Will?
poaAboutYou.a1: Your name, date of birth and address have to match on every legal document. We take them from your Will so you only type them once. Change them in your Will and they change here too.
poaAboutYou.q2: Do I need to finish my Will first?
poaAboutYou.a2: No. You only need the About You details: your name, date of birth, address and province.
poaAboutYou.a3: Each province has its own law for this document: its name, when it can take effect and who may witness it. We follow the rules of the province you live in.

poaAttorneys.a1: Any adult you trust who is able to manage money. Most people choose a spouse, an adult child or a close friend. They don't need to be a lawyer or live nearby, though it helps if they can reach your bank easily.
poaAttorneys.q2: How many attorneys can I name?
poaAttorneys.a2: Up to three. One is simplest. Two or three share the work, and you'll choose whether they decide together or each can act alone.
poaAttorneys.a3: Yes. It's a real responsibility. Ask each person, and tell them where you'll keep the signed document.
poaAttorneys.q4: Can my attorney take my money for themselves?
poaAttorneys.a4: No. The law requires them to act honestly, in your interest, and to keep records. Misusing your money can be a crime.

poaDecision.a1: Every decision needs all of them to agree and sign. It's the safest choice, but slower, and if one can't act, the others may be stuck unless you name a backup.
poaDecision.q2: What does each acting alone mean?
poaDecision.a2: Any one of them can act on their own. It's convenient, especially if they live apart, but each has full power without checking with the others.
poaDecision.a3: Most people choose together for safety. If your attorneys live far apart or you need things done quickly, each acting alone can be easier.

poaBackups.a1: If your attorney dies, becomes ill or doesn't want to act, your backup steps in. Without one, your family may need to go to court.
poaBackups.a2: Only if the people you named first can't or won't act. They take over with the same powers.
poaBackups.q3: Can I name more than one backup?
poaBackups.a3: Yes, up to three, in order. The second only acts if the first can't.

poaEffective.q1: What's the difference between the two options?
poaEffective.a1: Effective now means your attorney can help as soon as it's signed, even while you're well, for example if you're travelling. On incapacity means it only works once a doctor or nurse practitioner confirms you can't manage your affairs.
poaEffective.q2: Why can't I choose in my province?
poaEffective.a2: Some provinces allow only one option. In Nova Scotia a power of attorney takes effect when it's signed. In Québec a protection mandate only takes effect once you're incapable and a court has confirmed it.
poaEffective.a3: It gives your attorney power straight away, so only choose it if you trust them fully. Many people sign it now and keep the original somewhere safe until it's needed.

poaLimits.q1: Do I need to add limits?
poaLimits.a1: No. Most people leave this blank, which gives their attorney the full powers the law allows.
poaLimits.q2: What kind of limits can I add?
poaLimits.a2: For example: "Don't sell my cottage", or "Ask my daughter before any gift over $1,000". Keep them short and clear.
poaLimits.q3: What's the difference between limits and instructions?
poaLimits.a3: Limits restrict what your attorney may do. Instructions are wishes they should follow, like keeping your home as long as possible.
poaLimits.q4: Will my words be printed as I type them?
poaLimits.a4: Yes, word for word. A lawyer can check that they say what you mean.

poaCompensation.a1: It's your choice. Family members often act for free. For a lot of work over many years, payment can be fair.
poaCompensation.a2: Your attorney can always be repaid, from your money, for reasonable expenses such as postage, travel or fees.
poaCompensation.q3: How much would they be paid?
poaCompensation.a3: Only what your province's law allows. In Ontario it follows a set fee scale; elsewhere it must be reasonable, and a court can review it.

poaWitnesses.q1: Why do the witness rules matter?
poaWitnesses.a1: If the wrong person witnesses it, the document may not be valid. We show the rules for your province so you can pick the right people.
poaWitnesses.q2: Who is usually a good witness?
poaWitnesses.a2: An adult friend, neighbour or colleague who isn't your attorney, isn't related to your attorney and doesn't benefit from the document.
poaWitnesses.q3: Do the witnesses need to read it?
poaWitnesses.a3: No. They watch you sign and then sign themselves. They don't need to know what it says.
poaWitnesses.q4: Can I sign it at a lawyer's office?
poaWitnesses.a4: Yes. A lawyer or notary can witness it and answer your questions. In some provinces a lawyer is the easiest witness to use.

directiveAboutYou.q1: Why do you use the details from my Will?
directiveAboutYou.a1: Your name, date of birth and address must match on every legal document. We take them from your Will so you only type them once.
directiveAboutYou.q2: Do I need to finish my Will first?
directiveAboutYou.a2: No. You only need the About You details: your name, date of birth, address and province.
directiveAboutYou.a3: Each province has its own law for this document: its name, what your decision-maker is called and who may witness it. We follow the rules of the province you live in.

directiveDecisionMakers.a1: If you can't make or communicate a health or personal care decision, they make it for you, following the wishes in this document and what they know of your values.
directiveDecisionMakers.a2: An adult who knows you well, will respect your wishes even if they'd choose differently, and can be reached quickly in an emergency. Many people choose a spouse, an adult child or a close friend.
directiveDecisionMakers.a3: Yes. Talk to them about your wishes, and make sure they're willing. It's a hard role in a hard moment.
directiveDecisionMakers.q4: Can my doctor be my decision-maker?
directiveDecisionMakers.a4: Usually not. Most provinces don't let a paid care provider act for you unless they're also family. Choose someone close to you instead.

directiveDecision.a1: They must agree on each decision. It's careful, but can be slow in an emergency, and they may disagree.
directiveDecision.q2: What does each deciding alone mean?
directiveDecision.a2: Whoever is available can decide. It's quicker in an emergency, which is why some people choose it for health care.
directiveDecision.a3: Many people name one decision-maker and a backup, which avoids the question. With two or more, most choose together.

directiveBackups.a1: If your decision-maker can't be reached, is ill or doesn't want to act, your backup steps in. Without one, the law picks someone from your family, in a set order.
directiveBackups.a2: Only if the people you named first can't or won't act. They follow the same wishes.
directiveBackups.q3: Can I name more than one backup?
directiveBackups.a3: Yes, up to three, in order.

directiveLifeSupport.a1: Machines and treatments that keep you alive when your body can't: a breathing machine, tube feeding, dialysis. This question is about when there's no reasonable hope that you'll recover.
directiveLifeSupport.a2: CPR, electric shocks and a breathing tube if your heart or breathing stops. It can save lives, but for someone very ill it rarely works and can cause injury.
directiveLifeSupport.a3: Choose to let your decision-maker decide. They'll talk to your doctors and do what they believe you'd want.
directiveLifeSupport.q4: Is this the same as a do-not-resuscitate order?
directiveLifeSupport.a4: No. A DNR order is written by your doctor for the care you're receiving now. Your directive guides it, so talk to your doctor too.

directiveComfort.q1: Will pain relief shorten my life?
directiveComfort.a1: Good pain relief rarely shortens life. Stronger medicine can make you drowsy, which is why we ask whether comfort or staying alert matters more to you.
directiveComfort.a2: Care that focuses on comfort and dignity near the end of life, in a hospice, a hospital unit or at home.
directiveComfort.q3: What should I put in the note?
directiveComfort.a3: Anything your decision-maker and doctors should know: a treatment you'd never want, music you'd like, who you'd want with you. It's printed as you type it.

directiveValues.a1: No document can foresee every situation. Knowing what matters to you helps your decision-maker choose as you would.
directiveValues.q2: What about religious or cultural wishes?
directiveValues.a2: Write any practice or belief your care should respect: food, prayer, rituals at the end of life, who should be present, or treatments your faith doesn't allow.
directiveValues.q3: Do I have to fill this in?
directiveValues.a3: No. It's optional, and you can leave it blank.

directiveDonation.q1: Is recording my wish here enough?
directiveDonation.a1: Not on its own. Hospitals check your province's donor registry. Register there too, and tell your family, who are usually asked to confirm.
directiveDonation.q2: Can I donate if I'm older or unwell?
directiveDonation.a2: Often, yes. Doctors decide at the time what can be donated. Don't rule yourself out.
directiveDonation.a3: Nova Scotia presumes that adults agree to donate unless they've registered a decision not to. Record your decision on the registry either way.
directiveDonation.q4: Does donation affect my care or funeral?
directiveDonation.a4: No. Doctors try to save your life first, and an open-casket funeral is usually still possible.

directiveWitnesses.q1: Why do the witness rules matter?
directiveWitnesses.a1: If the wrong person witnesses it, the document may not be valid. We show the rules for your province so you can pick the right people.
directiveWitnesses.q2: My province doesn't require a witness. Should I use one?
directiveWitnesses.a2: Yes, we recommend it. A witness makes it harder for anyone to question later whether you really signed it.
directiveWitnesses.q3: Who is usually a good witness?
directiveWitnesses.a3: An adult friend, neighbour or colleague who isn't your decision-maker, isn't married to them, and isn't your own spouse.

estateIntro.a1: A named item or amount to a named person, like “my watch to my son” or “$5,000 to my friend”.
estateIntro.q2: What is the rest of my estate?
estateIntro.a2: Everything left after debts, taxes and your gifts. For most people it's the largest part of what they leave.
estateIntro.q3: What happens to things I don't mention?
estateIntro.a3: They fall into the rest of your estate and are shared the way you choose there.
estateIntro.a4: The main plan is what you want to happen. The backup plan applies if your main beneficiary dies before you, and the last-resort plan only if everyone in the earlier plans has died.
estateIntro.q5: Where did my list of assets go?
estateIntro.a5: It's now in your Vault as an inventory for your executor. It isn't printed in your Will, but you can still leave any asset on it as a gift.

specificGifts.a1: A named item or amount to a named person, like “my watch to my son” or “$5,000 to my friend”.
specificGifts.q2: What if I sell a gifted item before I die?
specificGifts.a2: The gift fails and the person gets nothing in its place, unless you update your Will.
specificGifts.q3: Can I leave a gift to a child?
specificGifts.a3: Yes. The trusts step decides the age they receive it; until then it's held for them.
specificGifts.q4: What does “If they die before you” mean?
specificGifts.a4: It says where the gift goes if the person dies first: to their own children, back into the rest of your estate, or to someone you name.
specificGifts.q5: Do I need to list everything I own?
specificGifts.a5: No. Name only the things that matter to you. Everything else is covered by household items and the rest of your estate.

householdItems.a1: Furniture, clothing, jewellery, dishes, books and other personal belongings — not cash, investments, vehicles or real estate.
householdItems.q2: What if they go into the rest of my estate?
householdItems.a2: Your executor may sell, donate or give them away, and any money becomes part of the rest of your estate.
householdItems.q3: Can I leave some items to particular people?
householdItems.a3: Yes. Add them as specific gifts. Everything else follows the choice you make here.
householdItems.q4: How will my children divide them?
householdItems.a4: Your executor divides them as evenly as is practical. Many families agree among themselves first.

charityGifts.q1: Why give to charity in a Will?
charityGifts.a1: It supports a cause you care about, and your estate can get a tax credit that reduces the final tax bill.
charityGifts.q2: Can I leave a percentage instead?
charityGifts.a2: Yes. Add the charity in the next step, “The rest of your estate”, and give it a share.
charityGifts.q3: Can I direct it to a program?
charityGifts.a3: Yes. Name the program; the charity decides whether it can honour the direction.
charityGifts.q4: Why do you ask for the registration number?
charityGifts.a4: It identifies the charity with the CRA so there's no confusion, and your executor needs it for the tax receipt.

residue.q1: What is the rest of my estate?
residue.a1: Everything left after debts, taxes and your specific gifts. It's usually most of your estate.
residue.q2: Percentages or shares — which should I use?
residue.a2: Percentages must add up to 100. Shares are easier when you add people: 2 shares and 1 share means two thirds and one third.
residue.q3: What if someone dies before me?
residue.a3: Each person has a choice: their part goes to their own children, to the others in this list, or to someone you name.
residue.q4: Do I have to provide for my spouse or children?
residue.a4: Dependants may have a legal right to support from your estate even if your Will leaves them out. The rules vary by province.
residue.q5: Can a charity share in the rest of my estate?
residue.a5: Yes. Add the charity as one of the people sharing it.

planSummary.q1: What if this plan can't be carried out?
planSummary.a1: Your backup and last-resort plans cover it. If nothing applies, provincial intestacy rules decide who inherits.
planSummary.a2: Yes. Edit any part now, or update your Will whenever your life changes.
planSummary.q3: Why don't all my assets show here?
planSummary.a3: Your full inventory lives in the Vault. Only the assets you chose as gifts appear in your plan.

backupPlan.q1: Why do I need a backup plan?
backupPlan.a1: If your main beneficiary dies before you, the backup plan says who inherits instead.
backupPlan.q2: What does “survive me by 30 days” mean?
backupPlan.a2: A beneficiary must outlive you by 30 days, so your estate doesn't pass through someone who dies soon after you.
backupPlan.q3: Is this different from “If they die before you”?
backupPlan.a3: Yes. That choice covers one gift or share. The backup plan replaces your whole main plan.

lastResort.q1: When would the last-resort plan be used?
lastResort.a1: Only if everyone in your earlier plans has died — for example, in a shared accident.
lastResort.a2: Provincial intestacy rules would decide who gets that part of your estate.
lastResort.a3: Often siblings, nieces and nephews, close friends, or a charity.

trusts.a1: Minors can't legally receive an inheritance. A trust lets a trustee manage it until the age you choose.
trusts.a2: Your executor by default, acting as trustee.
trusts.q3: What can the trustee spend it on?
trusts.a3: The young person's care, education and support before the payout age.
trusts.a4: Paying in parts, such as a third at 21, 25 and 30, so a young adult doesn't receive everything at once.
trusts.q5: What about a family member with a disability?
trusts.a5: A Henson trust or an RDSP can protect their government benefits. These need a lawyer's advice.

familyCheck.a1: Spouses, children and other dependants may have a legal right to support from your estate even if your Will leaves them out.
familyCheck.q2: Can I leave someone $1 to disinherit them?
familyCheck.a2: It doesn't stop a dependant's claim. Get legal advice if you plan to leave out a dependant.
familyCheck.a3: Usually a spouse, a common-law partner and children you support. The rules vary by province.
familyCheck.q4: Is my reason printed in the Will?
familyCheck.a4: No. It's kept privately with your answers so your executor can understand your choice.

debtsTaxes.a1: Your executor pays them from your estate before anything is given out. Your beneficiaries aren't personally responsible for them.
debtsTaxes.q2: What about taxes owed at death?
debtsTaxes.a2: A final tax return is filed for the year you die, and the estate may owe tax on investments and property. Your executor handles this, often with an accountant.
debtsTaxes.q3: Do RRSPs, TFSAs and life insurance follow my Will?
debtsTaxes.a3: Not if they name a beneficiary. That designation usually wins over your Will, so check it matches your wishes.
debtsTaxes.q4: What happens to a mortgage on a property I give away?
debtsTaxes.a4: You choose: the person takes the property with the mortgage, or your executor pays it off from the estate first.

optionalClauses.q1: What does the digital assets clause do?
optionalClauses.a1: It lets your executor access and close your online accounts, photos and cryptocurrency.
optionalClauses.q2: What does the RESP clause do?
optionalClauses.a2: It tells your executor how to keep or close education savings plans you hold for a child.
optionalClauses.q3: What does the charity payments clause do?
optionalClauses.a3: A charity's receipt is enough to show your executor paid a gift, so they don't have to check how the charity uses it.
optionalClauses.a4: It discourages challenges by removing gifts from anyone who contests the Will. Courts don't always enforce it.
optionalClauses.a5: They're simply ignored if they don't apply, and they save your executor trouble if they do.

provinceSelection.q1: Why does my province matter for my Will?
provinceSelection.a1: Will requirements differ by province — the number of witnesses, witnessing rules, and estate administration procedures all depend on where you live.
provinceSelection.q2: What if I own property in more than one province?
provinceSelection.a2: Your Will is governed by the province where you live when you sign it. If you own real estate elsewhere, a local estate lawyer may need to be involved for that property.
provinceSelection.q3: Can I change my province after starting my Will?
provinceSelection.a3: Yes. Update it in Settings → Province, then review your Will carefully — witness requirements and the age of majority may change.

personalInfo.a1: Your full legal name as it appears on your government ID, so your executor can prove the Will is yours.
personalInfo.q2: Why do you ask for pronouns?
personalInfo.a2: Only to word the document correctly, for example "his" or "their" estate.
personalInfo.q3: What if I have homes in two places?
personalInfo.a3: Use the province where you live most of the year; that usually decides which law applies.

previousWills.q1: What does it mean to revoke a Will?
previousWills.a1: Revoking a Will simply cancels it. The clause in your new Will that revokes earlier ones makes sure only your latest wishes count.
previousWills.q2: Why would I keep a Will from another country?
previousWills.a2: If you own a home or accounts abroad, a Will made there under local law can make things easier for your family. Get advice in both places so neither Will accidentally cancels the other.
previousWills.q3: I've never had a Will. Does this still matter?
previousWills.a3: Not really. Keep the first option: the clause is standard and does no harm when there is nothing to cancel.

foreignWills.q1: Why do you ask which countries?
foreignWills.a1: It records that other Wills exist and where they were made, so they can be kept in step with this one and your executor knows to look for them.
foreignWills.q2: Do I need a lawyer in the other country?
foreignWills.a2: We strongly recommend it. Local law decides whether your foreign Will stays valid next to this one, and a lawyer there can check its wording.
foreignWills.q3: What if I own property abroad but have no Will there?
foreignWills.a3: Then you can go back and cancel all previous Wills. Your Canadian Will can still cover property abroad, although some countries apply their own rules to real estate.

family.q1: Should I list children I'm not leaving anything to?
family.a1: Yes. Listing them shows you thought of them and lets the rest of your Will adapt. Nobody receives anything unless you choose it later.
family.q2: Does "married" include common-law and same-sex partners?
family.a2: A same-sex marriage is a marriage. If you live together without being married, choose common-law: each province treats common-law partners a little differently.
family.q3: What if my family changes later?
family.a3: Update your Will whenever it does. In some provinces a marriage or a divorce can cancel all or part of an existing Will automatically.
family.q4: What counts as a legal guardianship?
family.a4: A court order or other legal arrangement that makes you responsible for someone, such as a niece you are raising or an adult in your care.

separated.q1: Does separation cancel my spouse's rights?
separated.a1: Not always. Some provinces treat a separated spouse as if you had divorced, others only once the divorce is final. That is why the choice is yours here.
separated.q2: Should I name my spouse anyway?
separated.a2: Name them if you still want to leave them something or give them a role. Naming them doesn't mean they receive anything; that is decided later.
separated.a3: Yes. Come back to this screen at any time, and update your Will once your separation is settled.

spouse.q1: Which name should I use for my spouse?
spouse.a1: Their full legal name as it appears on their government ID, so there is no doubt about who you mean.
spouse.q2: Why do you ask how to describe them?
spouse.a2: The Will refers to them as your wife, husband or partner. Pick the word you want in the document.
spouse.q3: Why do you ask for their pronouns?
spouse.a3: Only to word the document correctly. You can leave it blank.

children.a1: Yes. Legally adopted children are treated exactly like birth children.
children.a2: They don't inherit automatically. Name them in a gift, or turn on "Treat my stepchildren as my children".
children.q3: Can I include a child who isn't born yet?
children.a3: Leave "Include children born or adopted after I sign" on and they'll be covered.
children.q4: Why do you need birth dates?
children.a4: To know who is a minor and will need a guardian or a trust.

grandchildren.a1: So your Will can pass a share on to a grandchild if their parent dies before you, or leave them a gift of their own.
grandchildren.a2: No. Listing them doesn't give them anything unless you choose to.
grandchildren.q3: Why do you need birth dates?
grandchildren.a3: A grandchild who is still a minor can't take a gift outright, so it may need to be held for them until they're older.

wards.q1: Who counts as someone in my guardianship?
wards.a1: Anyone a court or legal order has made you responsible for, such as a niece you are raising.
wards.q2: What happens to them if I die?
wards.a2: Guardianship doesn't pass on by itself. If they're a minor, your Will can name who you'd like to care for them.
wards.a3: An adult in your care won't need a guardian in your Will, but you can still leave them a gift.

deceasedFamily.q1: Why name family members who have died?
deceasedFamily.a1: It shows you remembered them, and it tells your executor whether the children of a child who died before you should take that child's share.
deceasedFamily.q2: Should I list parents or siblings who have died?
deceasedFamily.a2: Only if it helps explain your family. A spouse or a child who has died matters most.
deceasedFamily.q3: Will they appear in my Will?
deceasedFamily.a3: Only where a name is needed to make a gift clear.

otherPeople.a1: A class of people, such as "my nieces and nephews". It includes anyone who joins the group later, like a niece born after you sign.
otherPeople.q2: How do I name a charity?
otherPeople.a2: Use its legal name and its CRA registration number, so there's no doubt which charity you mean.
otherPeople.q3: Do I have to add everyone now?
otherPeople.a3: No. You can add people and charities when you reach each gift.

executors.a1: They gather everything you own, pay your debts and taxes, and then hand out what's left exactly as your Will says.
executors.q2: Can my executor also inherit from me?
executors.a2: Yes. It's very common to name someone who is also receiving part of your estate, like a spouse or an adult child.
executors.q3: Should I name more than one?
executors.a3: One is the simplest. Co-executors usually have to agree on everything, which can slow things down if they don't get along or live far apart.
executors.q4: Does my executor have to live in my province?
executors.a4: No. But someone living elsewhere may have to post a bond, a kind of insurance the court asks for, and will find the job harder from a distance.
executors.a5: They can claim reasonable pay for their work, set by provincial rules and often a small percentage of the estate. Many family members choose not to.
executors.a6: If your executor dies, can't act or says no and there's no backup, a court decides who settles your estate. That takes longer and costs more.

backupExecutors.q1: When does a backup step in?
backupExecutors.a1: Only if your executor dies before you, can't act when the time comes, or turns the job down.
backupExecutors.q2: What's the difference between backups in order and a group?
backupExecutors.a2: Backups in order step in one at a time, in the order you list them. A group steps in all at once and makes decisions together.
backupExecutors.q3: Can a backup also inherit from me?
backupExecutors.a3: Yes, just like your main executor.

guardians.q1: If I die, won't my children's other parent automatically take over?
guardians.a1: Usually, yes. A surviving parent with custody normally keeps caring for the children, and a guardian named in your Will steps in only if that parent can't. Naming one still matters in case you both die, or the other parent isn't able to.
guardians.q2: Does the court have to follow my choice?
guardians.a2: Not strictly. A court decides what's best for each child and treats your Will as strong evidence of your wishes. A guardian you've named who clearly cares for the children is rarely passed over.
guardians.q3: Should my children share one guardian?
guardians.a3: Most families choose one guardian so brothers and sisters grow up together. A different guardian for each child can make sense for older children from different relationships, or a child with particular needs.
guardians.q4: Will the guardian also look after my children's inheritance?
guardians.a4: Not by default. Raising a child and managing their money are separate roles. Your executor or a trustee usually holds the money, though the same person can do both if you choose them for both.
guardians.q5: Should I ask the person first?
guardians.a5: Yes. Raising someone else's children is a big commitment. Talk to them before you name them, and again if your circumstances change.
guardians.q6: Can I name a couple, and what if they split up?
guardians.a6: Yes. You can appoint two people to act together, such as your sister and her husband. Because couples sometimes separate, the Will also says which of them carries on alone if that happens.
guardians.q7: Should the guardian also be my executor?
guardians.a7: It's up to you. Some people prefer to keep the two roles apart so decisions about money and daily care are shared out. Others trust one person with both.

pets.q1: Can I leave money to my pet?
pets.a1: No. The law treats animals as property, so they can't inherit. Your Will leaves your pet, and any money for its care, to the person you trust to look after it.
pets.a2: A rough guide is a year of food, vet visits and grooming, multiplied by the years your pet is likely to live. Keep it in proportion to the rest of your estate.
pets.q3: Does the caregiver have to spend the money on my pet?
pets.a3: Usually the money becomes theirs, so your wish rests on trust. Choose someone you're sure of. A lawyer can tell you whether a more formal arrangement is possible in your province.
pets.q4: What if I get a new pet after I sign?
pets.a4: Come back to this step and update your Will so the new pet is named. Until then, a pet that isn't listed is treated like the rest of your belongings.
pets.q5: Can a charity or rescue take my pet?
pets.a5: Yes. Some animal charities take in and rehome pets left to them. Contact them first, since many have their own forms and conditions.

beneficiaries.q1: What's the difference between a percentage and a specific asset?
beneficiaries.a1: A percentage means the person receives that share of whatever remains after debts and specific gifts. A specific asset gift is a named item that goes to one person regardless of the estate's total value.
beneficiaries.q2: What if a beneficiary dies before me?
beneficiaries.a2: Their share returns to the remaining estate by default. You can name a backup for each gift in the assets and residual-estate steps. The review screen shows any gifts with no backup.
beneficiaries.q3: Can I name a charity as a beneficiary?
beneficiaries.a3: Yes. Use the charity's full legal name and add them as a person with the relationship "Charity." Their share is treated the same as any other beneficiary's.

assets.q1: Do I need to list every single thing I own?
assets.a1: No. Focus on significant or sentimental items: real estate, investment accounts, vehicles, bank accounts, and personal items with clear value. Minor everyday property passes through your estate automatically.
assets.a2: Joint assets with a right of survivorship — such as a family home co-owned with a spouse — pass directly to the co-owner outside the Will. List them so your executor knows they exist, but they won't be distributed through the Will.
assets.q3: What happens to assets I forget to list?
assets.a3: They pass through your residual estate — the catch-all you define in the next step. It's a safety net, not a replacement for listing important items specifically.

residualEstate.a1: It is everything that remains after your debts are paid and all specific gifts are distributed. Named beneficiaries receive their share of whatever is left over.
residualEstate.q2: Do the percentages here need to add up to 100%?
residualEstate.a2: Yes. The total must be exactly 100% for the Will to be complete. If one recipient dies before you and you name no backup, their share needs to go somewhere — add a gift-over or redistribute.
residualEstate.q3: Should I include my spouse here?
residualEstate.a3: Many people name their spouse as 100% residual beneficiary, with adult children as backup. There is no right answer — it depends on your family situation and any estate-planning advice you've received.

wishes.a1: No, they guide your family. Share them now, because funerals often happen before the Will is read. That's why VeeWill keeps them as a separate memo rather than printing them in your Will.
wishes.q2: What is a letter of instructions?
wishes.a2: A private note for your executor: where to find accounts, documents and passwords' locations, and who to contact. It isn't part of your Will and can be updated anytime. Ticking the box adds a short clause that refers to it.
wishes.q3: Who sees my notes for loved ones?
wishes.a3: Only the person each note is for, when your Vault is released through your Release Settings. Notes are never printed in your Will.
wishes.q4: Can I change a note later?
wishes.a4: Yes. Edit or remove your notes here or in the Vault at any time. They don't affect your Will, so there's nothing to re-sign.
wishes.q5: How many notes can I leave?
wishes.a5: As many as you like. Both VeeWill plans include notes for loved ones.

help.heroSubtitle: Find answers to common questions about VeeWill and making a valid Will
help.searchNoResultsBody: Try different or fewer words, or ask our support team directly.
help.startQ1: What kind of Will does VeeWill create?
help.startA1: VeeWill prepares a formal, typed Will from your answers. You print it, then sign it in front of two witnesses. It is not a holograph (handwritten) Will, which must be written entirely in your own hand.
help.startQ2: Is a VeeWill Will legally valid in Canada?
help.startA2: Yes, once it is printed, signed by you and witnessed as your province requires. A Will that is only saved in the app, or signed electronically, is not valid. In Québec you can also make a notarial Will with a notary.
help.startA3: Yes. Sign in front of two adult witnesses who are present at the same time, and who then sign too. A witness should not be a beneficiary, or the spouse or partner of one, or that gift may be void.
help.billingQ1: What's the difference between the plans?
help.billingA1: The Will plan gives you your Will, notes for loved ones, your funeral wishes, Release Settings (who receives what after you die) and a year of updates. Complete Protection adds a Financial Power of Attorney, a Health Care Directive, the Vault, an executor file with a checklist for your executor, and up to 5 versions of your Will.
help.billingQ2: Can I update my Will after creating it?
help.billingA2: Yes. Edit your answers and download a new Will, then print, sign and witness it again. The newest signed Will replaces earlier ones. Every plan includes a year of VeeWill Membership, which is what lets you make changes; after that you can renew it for a year at a time.
help.billingQ3: What is Law Firm Signing Assistance?
help.billingA3: An optional service that connects you with a law firm in your province to review your ready-to-sign Will and supervise the signing and witnessing. It isn't required for a valid Will. Pricing varies by province.
help.executorQ1: How do I ensure my executor can access my Will?
help.executorA1: VeeWill's Digital Vault allows you to securely store your Will and grant access to your executor. You can configure release settings that automatically notify your executor and provide access based on triggers you define, such as manual release or inactivity periods.
help.executorQ2: What happens to my Will if I move provinces?
help.executorA2: A Will that was valid where you signed it generally stays valid after a move within Canada. Rules on spouses, witnesses and estate administration differ, though, so update your province in Settings and review your Will.
help.securityA1: Absolutely. VeeWill uses bank-level encryption to protect your data. Your personal information and Will documents are stored securely in the cloud, encrypted in transit and at rest, and only the people you choose in Release Settings can ever see them. We never share your data with third parties.
help.securityQ2: Can I get legal advice through VeeWill?
help.legalAdviceNote: VeeWill helps you prepare a Will, but it isn't a law firm and doesn't give personalized legal advice. For complex situations, such as a business, property outside Canada, or a family member with a disability, consult an estate planning lawyer.
help.billingQ4: What happens when my membership ends?
help.billingA4: Nothing is lost. You can still download every document you made, and your Vault and notes are still released to your executor and loved ones. Editing and adding new files pause until you renew. We remind you 30 days and 7 days before it ends, and renewal never happens by itself.

directiveWizard.witnessesQcNotary: In Québec, you can also make a protection mandate in front of a notary instead of witnesses. We don't produce that version.
directiveWizard.witnessesQcRamq: Your advance medical directives (the RAMQ form) are separate from this mandate and have their own signing rules.
directiveWizard.witnessesTip: Good choices: a neighbour, a colleague, or a friend who isn't named in your document and isn't married to anyone who is.
directiveWizard.signStepRepresentative: Each representative signs the representative section, in front of a witness, to accept the role.
directiveWizard.signStepQcHomologation: The mandate only takes effect later, once a court homologates it. Your mandatary applies for that if you become incapable.
directiveWizard.signStepQcRamq: For a refusal that care teams must follow, also complete the RAMQ's advance medical directives form.
directiveWizard.signStepOptional: Your province doesn't require witnesses, but signing in front of one is safer.
directiveWizard.signStepStore: Keep the signed original somewhere safe. Give copies to your decision-makers and your doctor, and tell your family where it is.
directiveWizard.signStepDonor: Register your organ donation decision with your province's registry.
